precipitating_event: Following the Democrat Party's 1954 re-election (57.6% of votes but 92.8% of seats), Adnan Menderes's government imposed press censorship, jailed journalists, and interfered with the judiciary and universities to entrench one-party dominance.
consequential_events: On 27 May 1960, 38 military officers led by Cemal Gürsel staged a coup, arresting the Menderes government; Menderes and two ministers were executed 16-17 September 1961, a new constitution passed by referendum on 9 July 1961, and elections on 15 October 1961 restored civilian multiparty rule.

precipitating_event: President Sukarno issued Presidential Decree No. 150 of 1959, unilaterally dissolving the elected Constituent Assembly and reinstating the powerful-executive 1945 Constitution, formally ending parliamentary democracy and launching "Guided Democracy."
consequential_events: After the failed 30 September Movement coup attempt against army generals (1 October 1965) was crushed by General Suharto, Sukarno signed the "Supersemar" order on 11 March 1966 transferring emergency powers to Suharto, who immediately banned the PKI; Suharto became acting president in March 1967 and full president in March 1968.

precipitating_event: In July 1958, Nkrumah's government enacted the Preventive Detention Act, permitting detention without trial for up to five years, used to jail opposition politicians and consolidate CPP dominance.
consequential_events: A 1964 referendum made the CPP the sole legal party and Nkrumah president for life; worsening economic conditions and repression culminated in the 24 February 1966 "Operation Cold Chop" military coup while Nkrumah was abroad, with the new National Liberation Council dissolving the CPP and Parliament and suspending the constitution.

precipitating_event: On 14 July 1958, the Free Officers led by Brigadier Abd al-Karim Qasim overthrew and killed King Faisal II, Crown Prince Abd al-Ilah, and PM Nuri al-Said, ending the Hashemite monarchy and founding the Republic of Iraq.
consequential_events: After a further coup in November 1963 unseated Qasim's Ba'athist-Nasserist successors, a final coup on 17 July 1968 led by Ahmed Hassan al-Bakr seized key government and military installations, establishing the Revolutionary Command Council and inaugurating over three decades of Ba'ath Party rule.

precipitating_event: Amid an AFPFL party split and political instability, Prime Minister U Nu invited army Chief of Staff Ne Win to form a "caretaker government" on 28 October 1958, promising to restore order and hold new elections.
consequential_events: Ne Win's caretaker government held elections in February 1960 and returned power to civilians, but on 2 March 1962 Ne Win staged a second, permanent coup, abolishing parliament and the constitution; by 4 July 1962 all other parties were banned in favor of the sole legal Burma Socialist Programme Party.

precipitating_event: Facing defeat by Fidel Castro's 26th of July Movement guerrillas, dictator Fulgencio Batista fled Cuba on 1 January 1959; Castro's forces entered Havana on 7-8 January and Castro became Prime Minister by mid-February 1959.
consequential_events: Through 1959-61 the revolutionary government nationalized private industry and land, postponed promised elections, and merged rival factions into the Integrated Revolutionary Organizations; Castro declared Cuba a socialist state on 1 May 1961 and publicly proclaimed himself Marxist-Leninist in December 1961.

precipitating_event: On 25 December 1959, General Phoumi Nosavan staged a bloodless coup in Vientiane, deploying tanks and paratroopers to seize effective control of government days after PM Phoui Sananikone had dropped Phoumi and other CDNI-aligned ministers from the cabinet.
consequential_events: A cycle of coups and counter-coups followed (Kong Le 1960, Phoumi's CIA-backed counter-coup and the Battle of Vientiane December 1960); Phoumi's final coup attempt collapsed by early February 1965 when General Kouprasith Abhay crushed it and forced Phoumi into exile in Thailand.

precipitating_event: On 7 November 1961, the military forced elected President Jose Maria Velasco Ibarra from office after he ordered arrest of his own vice president amid a tax-hike crisis, installing Vice President Carlos Julio Arosemena Monroy as constitutional successor.
consequential_events: Arosemena was overthrown on 11 July 1963 by a military junta led by Ramon Castro Jijon, which declared martial law and outlawed the Communist Party; the junta ruled by decree through 1964 amid harsh austerity measures.

precipitating_event: In the early morning of 16 May 1961, Major General Park Chung-hee led military units to seize Seoul, dissolving the National Assembly, imposing martial law, and ousting the elected government of PM Chang Myon and President Yun Posun.
consequential_events: The junta's Supreme Council for National Reconstruction consolidated control and drafted a new constitution, approved in a referendum on 17 December 1962 with over 78% support, paving the way for Park to convert military rule into a tightly controlled presidency.

precipitating_event: On 15 December 1960, King Mahendra used the Royal Nepalese Army to seize power, dismissing and imprisoning PM B.P. Koirala and his cabinet, dissolving the elected Parliament, and abrogating Nepal's 1959 constitution.
consequential_events: Mahendra announced the partyless Panchayat system in 1961, then formalized the new order via the Constitution of Nepal, 1962, which outlawed political parties and vested ultimate authority in the king.

precipitating_event: After the ruling Radicals lost heavily to Peronist-backed candidates in March 1962 provincial elections, army officers annulled the elections and forced elected President Arturo Frondizi from office and into detention on 29 March 1962.
consequential_events: Senate President Jose Maria Guido was installed as a provisional civilian president under military tutelage; his government kept the Peronist party proscribed from politics, continuing through the 1963 elections.

precipitating_event: Building on a March 1961 constitution stripping the National Assembly of its power to unseat the government, President Fulbert Youlou announced in August 1962 plans to merge Congo's parties into a single ruling party.
consequential_events: Youlou's push for one-party rule triggered a popular uprising forcing his resignation in 1963; successor Alphonse Massamba-Debat declared one-party rule by July 1964, before he too was overthrown by the military on 4 September 1968.

precipitating_event: The 1961 Greek legislative election was marred by widespread fraud and intimidation orchestrated by the army and "parakratos" deep-state network under a plan codenamed "Pericles," becoming known as the "elections of violence and fraud."
consequential_events: The 1965 royal Apostasia crisis destabilized parliamentary rule; on 21 April 1967 colonels led by Papadopoulos seized power in a coup, and the junta cemented its rule via a controlled September 1968 constitutional referendum.

precipitating_event: In December 1963 the CAR's National Assembly formally adopted a constitutional amendment entrenching a strong seven-year presidency, followed by Dacko's unopposed re-election on 5 January 1964.
consequential_events: On the night of 31 December 1965/1 January 1966, army commander Jean-Bedel Bokassa staged the bloodless Saint-Sylvestre coup, invalidating the 1959 constitution and dissolving the National Assembly.

precipitating_event: On 8 March 1963, the clandestine Military Committee of the Syrian Ba'ath Party seized power in the "March 8 Revolution" coup, ending Syria's post-colonial democratic experimentation and purging 90% of the officer corps.
consequential_events: Intra-Ba'athist rivalry produced further upheavals; on 13 November 1970 Defense Minister Hafez al-Assad staged the bloodless "Corrective Movement" coup against Salah Jadid, later purging the "Old Guard" and consolidating durable personal dictatorship.

precipitating_event: On 13 January 1963, former French army NCOs led by Emmanuel Bodjolle, Etienne Eyadema, and Kleber Dadjo seized government buildings in Lome and assassinated President Sylvanus Olympio.
consequential_events: The 1963 plotters installed civilian Nicolas Grunitzky, but on 13 January 1967 Eyadema staged a second coup ousting Grunitzky, banning parties and suspending the constitution; he formally assumed the presidency 14 April 1967.

precipitating_event: President Jorge Pacheco Areco declared a state of emergency in June 1968 amid unrest over his wage/price freeze, beginning a pattern of rule-by-emergency-decree against labor and the Tupamaros.
consequential_events: On 27 June 1973 President Juan Maria Bordaberry dissolved the General Assembly, suspended the constitution, banned trade unions, and ruled by decree with a military-dominated National Security Council, inaugurating the 1973-1985 civic-military dictatorship.

precipitating_event: On 1-2 November 1963, ARVN generals led by Duong Van Minh, with CIA foreknowledge, launched a coup that arrested and summarily executed President Ngo Dinh Diem and his brother Ngo Dinh Nhu, ending Diem's autocratic family rule amid the Buddhist crisis.
consequential_events: The Minh-led junta proved unstable; before dawn on 30 January 1964, General Nguyen Khanh staged a bloodless coup ousting Minh's junta without firing a shot.

precipitating_event: General Christophe Soglo, who first seized power in an October 1963 coup before handing the presidency to civilian leader Sourou-Migan Apithy in January 1964, staged a second coup on 27 November 1965 removing the fractious Apithy-Ahomadegbe power-sharing government.
consequential_events: A caretaker presidency under Tahirou Congacou gave way when Soglo formally installed himself as President of Dahomey on 22 December 1965, ruling through a military government until younger officers ousted him in December 1967.

precipitating_event: Vice President Rene Barrientos and Army commander Alfredo Ovando Candia launched a military uprising on 3 November 1964; by the evening all major military units backed the coup, and President Victor Paz Estenssoro was forced into exile in Lima.
consequential_events: Barrientos and Ovando ruled jointly as a military junta through 1965, suppressing striking miners and leftist opposition, entrenching military control that persisted until Barrientos's death in a 1969 helicopter crash.

precipitating_event: General Olimpio Mourao Filho launched a military rebellion in Minas Gerais on 31 March 1964; within two days the military controlled the country, Congress declared the presidency vacant, and President Joao Goulart went into exile on 4 April.
consequential_events: Congress installed coup leader General Humberto Castelo Branco as president; Institutional Act No. 2, issued 27 October 1965, abolished all existing political parties and imposed indirect elections, cementing military-dominated rule.

precipitating_event: The last remaining civilian member of the 1963 Triumvirate, Manuel Enrique Tavares Espaillat, resigned on 27 June 1964 amid continued repression of supporters of ousted elected president Juan Bosch, leaving Donald Reid Cabral as unelected de facto ruler.
consequential_events: Reid Cabral governed by decree for the remainder of 1964 without any election in prospect, imposing unpopular austerity measures and purging military officers not personally loyal to him.

precipitating_event: President Modibo Keita launched the "Active Revolution" on 22 August 1967, suspending the constitution and National Assembly and creating the National Committee for the Defense of the Revolution to rule by decree.
consequential_events: Amid economic hardship, Lieutenant Moussa Traore led a bloodless military coup on 19 November 1968 that overthrew and imprisoned Keita; Traore's junta promised elections that never materialized and he formally became president in 1969.

precipitating_event: National Guard officers led by Major Boris Martinez staged a coup on 11 October 1968, deposing democratically elected President Arnulfo Arias just ten days after his inauguration, suspending civil rights and installing a Provisional Junta.
consequential_events: An internal power struggle culminated on 23 February 1969, when Lt. Col. Omar Torrijos exiled rival strongman Boris Martinez, consolidating personal control over the National Guard and inaugurating a personalist military dictatorship lasting until 1989.

precipitating_event: The March 1969 parliamentary elections were fraud-ridden and violent, with more than 25 people killed in election-related violence amid widespread allegations of fraud, deepening perceptions that the ruling Somali Youth League was becoming authoritarian.
consequential_events: President Abdirashid Ali Shermarke was assassinated on 15 October 1969; six days later General Siad Barre's Supreme Revolutionary Council seized power, dissolved parliament and the Supreme Court, and in 1970 declared Somalia a one-party socialist state.

precipitating_event: On 12 January 1964, 600-800 mainly African men led by John Okello launched an armed uprising that overthrew Sultan Jamshid bin Abdullah and his Arab-dominated government just a month after independence.
consequential_events: The new revolutionary government banished the Sultan, banned the opposition ZNP and ZPPP parties, installed Abeid Karume as President, and merged Zanzibar with Tanganyika in April 1964 to form Tanzania.

precipitating_event: A failed Hutu-officer coup attempt on 18-19 October 1965 opened a period of military instability that culminated on 8 July 1966, when Crown Prince Ndizeye's forces ousted PM Leopold Biha's government, suspended the constitution, and installed Ndizeye as King Ntare V with Michel Micombero as premier.
consequential_events: On 28 November 1966, PM Micombero ousted King Ntare V in a second coup, declared an end to the monarchy, and became the first President of the new Republic of Burundi.

precipitating_event: President Maurice Yameogo's government announced an austerity budget in December 1965 cutting salaries and raising taxes, then declared a state of emergency and deployed troops against a threatened general strike, provoking mass unrest.
consequential_events: Rank-and-file soldiers refused to fire on protesters, allowing Lt. Col. Sangoule Lamizana to force Yameogo's resignation, suspend the constitution, dissolve the National Assembly, and install a military-dominated council which continued consolidating control through 1967.

precipitating_event: A political impasse in which PM-designate Evariste Kimba lost a no-confidence vote but was reappointed anyway by President Kasa-Vubu caused governmental paralysis that Gen. Joseph Mobutu used to seize power on 25 November 1965, canceling scheduled elections while pledging to restore democracy.
consequential_events: Mobutu assumed near-dictatorial powers, framing his takeover as a five-year caretaker mission to restore democratic order -- a promise he never honored -- and by 1966 had abolished the prime ministership.

precipitating_event: On 19 June 1965, Defense Minister Col. Houari Boumedienne and allied army officers arrested President Ahmed Ben Bella in a bloodless pre-dawn coup, ending Ben Bella's increasingly personalist rule.
consequential_events: Boumedienne installed himself as Chairman of a new Revolutionary Council and by mid-1966 had reorganized the ruling FLN party, consolidating one-party military-backed rule with Ben Bella under house arrest until 1980.

precipitating_event: General Juan Carlos Ongania led the "Argentine Revolution," a military coup on 28 June 1966 that overthrew democratically elected President Arturo Illia, dissolved Congress, and banned all political parties, explicitly rejecting the label of a "provisional government."
consequential_events: The regime consolidated authoritarian rule via repression such as the "Night of the Long Batons" crackdown on university autonomy; Ongania was forced to resign in 1970 after the 1969 Cordobazo uprising.

precipitating_event: President Ferdinand Marcos, first elected 1965 and reelected 1969, signed Proclamation No. 1081 and announced martial law on 23 September 1972, suspending civil and political rights, abolishing Congress, and arresting opposition figures.
consequential_events: A Marcos-dominated Constitutional Convention approved a new charter, ratified by a lopsided plebiscite (95.27% in favor) in January 1973 via citizens' assemblies, formally entrenching Marcos's one-man rule; martial law was not lifted until 1981.

precipitating_event: On 22 February 1966 PM Milton Obote had five cabinet ministers arrested, then suspended Uganda's 1962 constitution and assumed all executive powers; a new "Revolutionary" constitution was pushed through parliament under military guard on 15 April 1966, abolishing the federal structure.
consequential_events: General Idi Amin overthrew Obote in a military coup on 25 January 1971 while Obote was abroad; Amin then purged roughly 5,000 soldiers from the Lango and Acholi ethnic groups by 1972, entrenching a more violent military dictatorship.

precipitating_event: Following the 17 March 1967 general election in which Siaka Stevens' opposition APC narrowly defeated the incumbent SLPP, Brigadier David Lansana staged a coup hours after Stevens was sworn in, arresting him and annulling the election result.
consequential_events: Dissenting officers arrested Lansana two days later and formed the National Reformation Council under Andrew Juxon-Smith, which vowed to restore democracy but ruled by decree for over a year until the 18 April 1968 "Sergeants' Coup" installed Siaka Stevens as elected PM.

precipitating_event: In the run-up to Guyana's 16 December 1968 general election, PM Forbes Burnham's PNC government, which controlled the electoral machinery, padded voter rolls and manipulated an opaque overseas/postal ballot process to manufacture a parliamentary majority despite Cheddi Jagan's PPP likely winning the domestic vote.
consequential_events: The fraud handed the PNC 30 of 53 seats and its first outright majority; it was exposed in two Granada Television documentaries and set the template for further rigged elections that entrenched PNC one-party dominance through the 1970s.

precipitating_event: In the early hours of 3 October 1968, General Juan Velasco Alvarado led an armored assault on the presidential palace, deposed and exiled elected President Fernando Belaunde amid an oil-contract scandal, and installed a military junta.
consequential_events: Within days the junta nationalized IPC's oil fields, defusing public opposition, and by 1969 was implementing a sweeping state-led "Peruvian Revolution" program including agrarian reform, confirming permanent revolutionary rule; the junta held power until 1980.

precipitating_event: PM Leabua Jonathan's ruling BNP lost the January 1970 election to Ntsu Mokhehle's BCP; before results were finalized, Jonathan declared a state of emergency, annulled the election, dissolved parliament, and suspended the constitution.
consequential_events: King Moshoeshoe II, who opposed the coup, was forced into exile for most of 1970; Jonathan then ruled by decree without an elected parliament for over a decade, until deposed in the 1986 military coup.

precipitating_event: Sino-Malay race riots erupted in Kuala Lumpur after opposition parties made major gains in the 1969 election; the government declared a state of emergency on 15-16 May 1969, suspended Parliament, and created the National Operations Council to rule by decree.
consequential_events: The NOC governed by decree for about 21 months; Parliament reconvened in February 1971, and constitutional amendments entrenched permanent restrictions on public discussion of "sensitive" issues even after normal rule resumed.

precipitating_event: Colonel Gaafar Nimeiry led the Free Officers Movement in a bloodless military coup on 25 May 1969, overthrowing the elected government, dissolving parliament, banning political parties, and establishing a Revolutionary Command Council.
consequential_events: The coup ended Sudan's second democratic era and installed Nimeiry as head of a new government; the regime pursued Nasserist Arab nationalism before Nimeiry consolidated one-man military rule that lasted 16 years.

precipitating_event: In a June 1969 constitutional referendum (85% in favor), Zambia removed the requirement that fundamental-rights amendments be approved by public referendum, allowing amendments via a two-thirds parliamentary majority alone.
consequential_events: In February 1972 Kaunda banned all opposition parties, making UNIP the sole legal party; a new constitution promulgated August 1973 formalized one-party rule, and single-candidate elections in December 1973 cemented one-party executive rule.

precipitating_event: Following a disputed 28 March 1970 election that gave regional pluralities to three rival politicians, Dahomey's leaders brokered a compromise on 7 May 1970 establishing a rotating three-person Presidential Council, each to serve two-year terms.
consequential_events: The Council survived a 1972 coup attempt and Maga's peaceful handover to Ahomadegbe-Tometin, but on 26 October 1972 Major Mathieu Kerekou seized power in a military coup, imprisoning all three council members and ending civilian power-sharing.

precipitating_event: President Jose Maria Velasco Ibarra, elected in 1968, suspended Congress in 1970 and began ruling by decree with military backing, effectively declaring himself dictator.
consequential_events: After Velasco's government promised elections for June 1972 in which populist favorite Assad Bucaram appeared likely to win, the military, anxious to control impending oil revenues, staged a coup on 15 February 1972 led by Gen. Guillermo Rodriguez Lara, arresting Velasco and deporting him to Panama.

precipitating_event: On 18 March 1970, Cambodia's National Assembly voted to withdraw confidence in Head of State Prince Norodom Sihanouk while abroad, following orchestrated demonstrations and pressure from PM Lon Nol; Sihanouk was formally deposed and Lon Nol assumed emergency powers, founding the Khmer Republic.
consequential_events: Lon Nol's 1972 "re-election" as president amid widespread fraud allegations entrenched his one-man rule; the Khmer Republic collapsed when Khmer Rouge forces captured Phnom Penh on 17 April 1975, ending the republic.

precipitating_event: PM J.R. Jayewardene's Second Amendment, passed 4 October 1977, converted the presidency into a powerful executive office he assumed personally in February 1978, and the full 1978 constitution granted the president sweeping, near-dictatorial powers.
consequential_events: A 1982 referendum extended the sitting parliament's term to 1989 rather than holding an election, while an amendment barred Tamil separatist-linked TULF MPs from parliament; Black July 1983 and the 1987-1989 JVP insurrection crackdown involved mass extrajudicial killings.

precipitating_event: On 7 May 1971, President Francisco Macias Nguema issued Decree 415, repealing parts of the 1968 constitution and granting himself all direct powers of Government, effectively suspending constitutional government; an accompanying law imposed the death penalty for threatening the president.
consequential_events: A new constitution approved by plebiscite on 29 July 1973 (99% approval) enshrined Macias Nguema's absolute power, following a July 1972 decree that had already declared him President for Life and merged all parties into his sole legal party.

precipitating_event: Following the Allahabad High Court's 12 June 1975 ruling that found PM Indira Gandhi guilty of electoral malpractice in her 1971 election and voided her seat, Gandhi had a national Emergency proclaimed just before midnight on 25 June 1975, suspending civil liberties and arresting opposition leaders within hours.
consequential_events: The Emergency, during which the press was censored and opposition figures jailed, was lifted on 21 March 1977 when Gandhi called fresh elections, in which her Congress party was defeated, restoring competitive politics.

precipitating_event: On 11 September 1973, a military junta led by General Augusto Pinochet launched a coup against elected President Salvador Allende amid escalating economic crisis and polarization; Allende died during the assault on La Moneda palace.
consequential_events: The junta banned political parties and began repression; Pinochet was proclaimed Supreme Chief of the Nation via decree in June 1974 and formally titled President of the Republic on 17 December 1974, consolidating personal dictatorial power lasting until 1990.

precipitating_event: On 13 January 1972, Colonel Ignatius Kutu Acheampong led a bloodless military coup that overthrew the elected government of PM Kofi Busia while Busia was abroad, suspending the constitution and installing the National Redemption Council.
consequential_events: The NRC ruled by decree through 1973, keeping the constitution suspended, parliament dissolved, and political parties banned, entrenching military rule until reorganized as the Supreme Military Council in 1975.

precipitating_event: Mass "Rotaka" protests in May 1972 forced President Philibert Tsiranana to transfer full executive power to army Chief of Staff General Gabriel Ramanantsoa, sidelining the elected civilian government.
consequential_events: An October 1972 referendum abolished the presidency and vested Ramanantsoa with sweeping powers for a five-year military-led transition, formally ending Madagascar's civilian First Republic.

precipitating_event: On 4-5 June 1977, armed SPUP supporters trained in Tanzania seized strategic sites on Mahe and ousted elected President James Mancham while he was abroad, installing SPUP leader France-Albert Rene as president.
consequential_events: Proclamations of June 1977 suspended and then revoked the constitution, vesting all legislative power in Rene by decree; a new 1979 constitution formalized one-party socialist rule, and Rene won the 1979 election unopposed.

precipitating_event: On 2 December 1972, General Oswaldo Lopez Arellano led a bloodless military coup that overthrew elected civilian President Ramon Ernesto Cruz, placing him under house arrest and ending Honduras's brief democratic interlude.
consequential_events: Lopez Arellano ruled by decree via a three-member military Defense Council; he was himself ousted in an internal military coup in April 1975 amid bribery allegations, with no return to elected civilian rule.

precipitating_event: On 5 July 1973, Army Chief of Staff Juvenal Habyarimana seized power in a military coup against President Gregoire Kayibanda, ousting the ruling Parmehutu party.
consequential_events: Military rule continued until 1975, when Habyarimana founded the MRND as Rwanda's sole legal party; a 1978 constitutional referendum formalized a one-party totalitarian state that he led unopposed through subsequent elections.

precipitating_event: On 12 April 1973, King Sobhuza II repealed Swaziland's Westminster-style independence constitution and dissolved parliament by royal decree, banning political parties and assuming absolute personal rule.
consequential_events: Sobhuza ruled by decree from 1973 until a 1978 constitution introduced the tinkhundla system of tribal councils, formalizing indirect royal control over representation and ending multiparty competition.

precipitating_event: On 28 August 1975, Emir Isa bin Salman Al Khalifa dissolved Bahrain's elected National Assembly after it refused to pass the government's proposed State Security Law, suspending the parliamentary provisions of the 1973 constitution.
consequential_events: Bahrain was governed by Emiri decree without an elected legislature for the remainder of Isa bin Salman's reign; the parliamentary system was never restored in his lifetime, with an elected legislature not reintroduced until 2002.

precipitating_event: President Isabel Peron declared a state of siege on 6 November 1975 suspending constitutional guarantees amid escalating guerrilla violence and the assassination of the Buenos Aires police chief.
consequential_events: On 24 March 1976 (Operation Aries) the armed forces arrested President Isabel Peron and installed a military junta led by Videla, formally named president 29 March 1976, launching the "Process of National Reorganization."

precipitating_event: In the early morning of 15 August 1975, junior army officers stormed the residence of President Sheikh Mujibur Rahman and assassinated him along with most of his family, installing an interim martial-law government.
consequential_events: After a counter-coup and the Sipahi-Janata mutiny that restored Ziaur Rahman as Army Chief, Zia formally consolidated military control by becoming Chief Martial Law Administrator on 29 September 1976.

precipitating_event: Following communist victories in Saigon and Phnom Penh, the Pathet Lao pressured rightist ministers to resign through mid-1975, dismantling the fragile 1973 coalition government from within.
consequential_events: A Congress of People's Representatives convened December 1975 formally abolished the Lao monarchy, forcing King Savang Vatthana's abdication, and proclaimed the Lao People's Democratic Republic under one-party communist rule.

precipitating_event: The NPS-led coalition government of PM Henck Arron finalized independence negotiations with the Netherlands, and independence was granted on 25 November 1975 amid controversial expropriations of Dutch-descended settlers' property.
consequential_events: In the run-up to and aftermath of independence, roughly a third of Suriname's population emigrated to the Netherlands amid fears the new country would not be viable, marked by social unrest and economic depression.

precipitating_event: Amid conflict between Emir Sabah Al-Salim Al-Sabah's government and an assertive National Assembly, the Emir issued a decree on 29 August 1976 suspending four constitutional articles governing press freedom and legislative dissolution, and dissolved the National Assembly outright.
consequential_events: The constitution and National Assembly remained suspended for roughly five years, with parliamentary life only reinstated in 1981.

precipitating_event: On 6 October 1976, Thai police and paramilitaries violently crushed a student protest at Thammasat University (the "6 October massacre"), and that same day the military under Admiral Sangad Chaloryu seized power from the elected government, installing royalist judge Thanin Kraivichien as PM.
consequential_events: On 20 October 1977, Sangad again seized power and forced Thanin's resignation, citing that Thanin's government had "divided the country" and had virtually no public support; General Kriangsak Chamanan was installed as the new PM.

precipitating_event: Army Chief Gen. Muhammad Zia-ul-Haq launched "Operation Fair Play," a bloodless coup against elected PM Zulfikar Ali Bhutto amid a crisis over opposition allegations of massive rigging in the March 1977 elections. Zia suspended the constitution and promised "free and fair elections" within 90 days.
consequential_events: Instead of the promised 90-day elections, Zia pursued a criminal case against Bhutto; the Lahore High Court sentenced Bhutto to death March 1978 (executed April 1979), and elections were delayed until 1985.

precipitating_event: Col. Mustafa Ould Salek led junior officers in a bloodless coup against founding President Moktar Ould Daddah, driven by military exhaustion from the Western Sahara War and Daddah's threats to hold officers accountable for corruption.
consequential_events: The junta imprisoned Daddah and dissolved one-party rule with no timetable for civilian rule; Daddah was exiled to France in August 1979, and Mauritania entered a prolonged period of serial military coups.

precipitating_event: PM Ian Smith signed the "Internal Settlement" with hand-picked, non-militant Black leaders, creating a transitional biracial Executive Council while excluding the actual insurgent opposition (Patriotic Front) from the transition.
consequential_events: Despite adding Black ministers, civil service, judiciary, police, and armed forces stayed under predominantly white officials; the resulting April 1979 elections excluded the Patriotic Front and were declared "null and void" by the UN.

precipitating_event: Col. Saye Zerbo led a bloodless coup ousting President Lamizana amid drought/famine-driven economic desperation and a wave of strikes, immediately following a failed no-confidence motion.
consequential_events: Zerbo suspended the constitution and installed a 31-member junta with no timetable for elections; the initially union-friendly regime turned repressive, imposing mandatory military service in May 1981 and banning strikes.

precipitating_event: Master Sgt. Samuel Doe led indigenous soldiers storming the Executive Mansion and killing President Tolbert, capping resentment of Americo-Liberian elite rule inflamed by 1979 rice-price riots.
consequential_events: Doe's People's Redemption Council publicly executed 13 Tolbert-era officials in April 1980; consolidation continued in 1981 as the regime executed alleged coup plotters within the junta itself in August 1981.

precipitating_event: Sgt.-Maj. Desi Bouterse led 16 NCOs in a coup against elected PM Henck Arron's government, triggered when Arron refused to recognize an NCO union and arrested its leaders.
consequential_events: The military initially retained civilian President Ferrier and installed a PM figurehead, but forced Ferrier's resignation in August 1980, continuing consolidation through 1981 before dismissing the figurehead outright in February 1982.

precipitating_event: On 12 September 1980, General Kenan Evren led the Turkish Armed Forces in a coup; the National Security Council abolished parliament, suspended the 1961 constitution, and banned all political parties and trade unions.
consequential_events: The junta's new constitution was approved by referendum November 1982, and power was handed to a civilian government after elections on 6 November 1983, ending three years of direct military rule during which ~650,000 people were arrested.

precipitating_event: On 31 December 1981, Flight Lieutenant Jerry Rawlings led his second coup, overthrowing the elected government of President Hilla Limann amid economic crisis, and installed the Provisional National Defence Council with himself as chairman.
consequential_events: The PNDC abolished the 1979 constitution, banned political parties, and consolidated military-backed rule, surviving counter-coup attempts; PNDC rule lasted 11 years until the 1992 constitution restored multiparty democracy.

precipitating_event: On 24 March 1982, Army Chief Gen. Hussain Muhammad Ershad forced President Abdus Sattar to resign, declared martial law, suspended the constitution, and banned political parties, installing a figurehead civilian president.
consequential_events: Ershad formally assumed the presidency himself in December 1983, replacing the figurehead president and consolidating personal military rule that continued until 1990.

precipitating_event: On 31 December 1983, Major General Muhammadu Buhari led a military coup that overthrew the elected government of President Shehu Shagari, following a firefight between coup plotters and the presidential guard.
consequential_events: The Buhari-led Supreme Military Council suspended the 1979 constitution, banned political parties, and ruled by decree, before Buhari was overthrown in a further coup by General Ibrahim Babangida in August 1985.

precipitating_event: In 1986, amid strained oil revenues and friction between the ruling family and elected deputies, Emir Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah suspended Kuwait's 1962 constitution and dissolved the National Assembly, ruling by decree through the Council of Ministers.
consequential_events: The suspension provoked a pro-democracy movement; under domestic and Gulf War-era international pressure the Emir agreed in October 1990 to restore constitutional rule, with elections finally held in October 1992.

precipitating_event: On 3 September 1987, Major Pierre Buyoya led a bloodless military coup that deposed President Bagaza while he was abroad at a summit; Buyoya suspended the constitution and formed a Military Committee for National Salvation.
consequential_events: Ethnic violence erupted in August 1988, with roughly 20,000 Hutu killed in military reprisals; Buyoya was proclaimed president in September 1988 and in October 1988 appointed a mixed civilian-military government under a Hutu prime minister.

precipitating_event: On 14 May 1987, Lt. Col. Sitiveni Rabuka led armed soldiers into Fiji's House of Representatives and forced PM Timoci Bavadra's newly elected multiracial coalition government to leave in a bloodless military coup.
consequential_events: A second coup on 25 September 1987 scuttled a negotiated power-sharing accord; Rabuka declared Fiji a republic on 7 October 1987, and a civilian interim government under Ratu Sir Kamisese Mara was installed in December 1987.

precipitating_event: On 30 June 1989, Brigadier General Omar al-Bashir, backed by Hassan al-Turabi's National Islamic Front, led a bloodless military coup overthrowing the elected government, dissolving parliament and suspending the constitution.
consequential_events: Al-Bashir established the Revolutionary Command Council; through 1989-1990 the regime banned all political parties and civil society bodies, purged tens of thousands from the army, police and civil service, and built a network of clandestine detention centers.

precipitating_event: On 5 April 1992, elected President Alberto Fujimori announced he was dissolving Congress and "reorganizing" the judiciary, deployed army tanks to Congress, and issued a decree suspending the constitution amid gridlock with an opposition-controlled Congress.
consequential_events: Fujimori called elections for a Democratic Constituent Congress held November 1992, which his supporters won; the new congress drafted a constitution approved by referendum in October 1993.

precipitating_event: Following restoration of independence in August 1991, Estonia's Supreme Council restored the 1938 citizenship law, automatically granting citizenship only to pre-1940 citizens and their descendants; Soviet-era Russian-speaking settlers did not automatically become citizens.
consequential_events: Roughly 30% of Estonia's population was left without citizenship in the first years of independence; the new constitution was approved by referendum 28 June 1992, and the September 1992 elections were conducted under the citizen-only franchise this policy created.

precipitating_event: On 24 December 1990 (the "telephone coup"), acting military commander Ivan Graanoogst phoned President Ramsewak Shankar to inform him he was deposed, driven by former strongman Desi Bouterse reasserting military dominance.
consequential_events: The government was dismissed 27 December 1990, the National Assembly dissolved, and Johan Kraag installed as interim president; the Netherlands suspended aid and international pressure forced observed elections in May 1991, won by Ronald Venetiaan.

precipitating_event: On 23 February 1991, a military junta led by General Sunthorn Kongsompong staged a bloodless coup, arresting PM Chatichai Choonhavan and ending Thailand's longest democratically elected government to that point.
consequential_events: King Bhumibol endorsed the coup on 26 February 1991; the junta formed the National Peace Keeping Council and appointed Anand Panyarachun as interim PM, drafting a new constitution preserving military influence.

precipitating_event: On January 11, 1992, Algeria's military forced President Chadli Bendjedid to resign and canceled the second round of elections the Islamic Salvation Front was poised to win, installing a High Council of State headed by Mohamed Boudiaf.
consequential_events: The FIS was banned and tens of thousands of supporters interned in desert camps; President Boudiaf was assassinated in June 1992; cancellation of the electoral process triggered a decade-long civil war.

precipitating_event: On the night of September 29-30, 1991, General Raoul Cedras and police chief Michel Francois led a military mutiny that attacked President Jean-Bertrand Aristide's residence, killed hundreds of civilians, and forced Aristide into exile.
consequential_events: The junta installed Joseph Nerette as provisional president October 1991 and through 1992 waged mass repression against Aristide supporters while resisting international sanctions.

precipitating_event: On September 7, 1992, opposition paramilitary forces captured President Rahmon Nabiyev and forced him at gunpoint to resign, amid a civil war between the government and a coalition of regional, Islamist, and democratic opposition forces.
consequential_events: The Supreme Soviet elected Emomali Rahmon as new leader in December 1992; Kulob-based militias backed by Russian and Uzbek forces waged what HRW described as ethnic cleansing against Pamiri and Garmi populations.

precipitating_event: On December 28, 1994, President Levon Ter-Petrosyan banned the opposition Armenian Revolutionary Federation, alleging a coup plot, raided its offices, and had 31 members arrested and later convicted.
consequential_events: In the September 25, 1996 presidential election, official results gave Ter-Petrosyan just above 50% amid widespread fraud allegations; roughly 200,000 protesters stormed parliament and were crushed by tanks and troops, and a minister later admitted the vote had been rigged.

precipitating_event: On June 4, 1993, military commander Surat Huseynov launched an armed mutiny from Ganja and marched on Baku, forcing President Abulfaz Elchibey to flee by June 18, ending his government.
consequential_events: Heydar Aliyev, recalled to power as parliament speaker, was elected president after an August 1993 referendum formally removed Elchibey, and progressively entrenched one-man, one-party dominance over the following years.

precipitating_event: On July 22, 1994, Lieutenant Yahya Jammeh led junior officers in a coup that overthrew long-serving elected President Dawda Jawara, dissolved the government, and abolished the constitution, publicly pledging a transition back to civilian democratic rule.
consequential_events: The junta shortened its planned transition, but by 1995-96 had banned key opposition parties and converted itself into the ruling APRC party ahead of the September 1996 election that confirmed Jammeh's rule.

precipitating_event: President Yeltsin issued a decree dissolving the Congress of People's Deputies on 21 September 1993; parliament impeached him, and the standoff culminated in the October 3-4, 1993 armed storming of the White House parliament building by government troops.
consequential_events: The December 1993 referendum created a super-presidential constitution; Putin's 2000s "power vertical" (abolition of elected governors, media/oligarch crackdowns, protest-law tightening) culminated in the March 2014 annexation of Crimea.

precipitating_event: The April 6, 1994 assassination of President Habyarimana triggered genocide against Tutsi and moderate Hutu, executed by a Hutu Power-led crisis committee that seized state control after the stalled 1993 Arusha power-sharing accords.
consequential_events: The RPF captured Kigali on July 4, 1994, ending the genocide; the new RPF-dominated government banned ethnically organized parties and "genocide ideology," establishing a de facto one-party state.

precipitating_event: The May 14, 1995 referendum granted President Lukashenko power to dissolve parliament for constitutional violations plus closer Russia ties, in a vote the OSCE found "violated international standards."
consequential_events: A second November 1996 referendum gave Lukashenko's decrees force of law, extended his term to 2001, and replaced the elected Supreme Soviet with a loyalist House of Representatives; the 2001 election, won amid OSCE findings the environment was "not democratic," cemented control.

precipitating_event: President Lissouba ordered his Cocoye militia to detain rival Sassou Nguesso and disarm his Cobra militia on June 5, 1997, fearing a coup, triggering civil war between the two factions.
consequential_events: With Angolan troops intervening on Sassou's behalf, Cobra militia forces took Brazzaville by October 16, 1997, and Sassou Nguesso declared himself president, ousting the elected Lissouba government by force.

precipitating_event: On August 17, 1994, King Letsie III, backed by military elements, staged a coup that suspended Parliament and installed an interim ruling council, ousting Ntsu Mokhehle's elected BCP government, demanding reinstatement of his father as head of state.
consequential_events: Under domestic protest and SADC mediation pressure, Letsie III reinstated Mokhehle's elected government on September 14, 1994; a negotiated settlement led Letsie III to abdicate in 1995 in favor of his father.

precipitating_event: On January 27, 1996, Colonel Ibrahim Bare Mainassara led a military coup in Niamey that deposed Niger's first democratically elected president, Mahamane Ousmane, and arrested PM Hama Amadou.
consequential_events: The junta reauthorized political parties and promised elections; Bare Mainassara nonetheless dissolved the independent National Electoral Commission to secure victory in the July 1996 election, and opposition boycotted the November 1996 legislative elections over the fraud.

precipitating_event: The Ortega-Aleman Pact, sealed January 2000 between FSLN leader Daniel Ortega and Liberal President Arnoldo Aleman, split control of the Supreme Court, Comptroller General, and Supreme Electoral Council between their two parties and lowered the winning threshold for president, entrenching a two-party duopoly.
consequential_events: After regaining the presidency in 2007, Ortega used a 2009 Supreme Court ruling and a 2014 constitutional amendment to abolish presidential term limits; his forces killed over 300 protesters in 2018, and in February 2025 a reform installed his wife as co-president.

precipitating_event: In the December 16, 2001 presidential election, the Ratsiraka-controlled electoral apparatus certified a count showing challenger Marc Ravalomanana with only 46%, a result disputed as manipulated to force a runoff Ratsiraka could contest from a stronger patronage position.
consequential_events: After months of parallel governments and regional blockades, Ratsiraka fled to the Seychelles on July 5, 2002, and Ravalomanana's forces took the last stronghold of Toamasina, ending the crisis with Ravalomanana recognized as president.

precipitating_event: President Leonid Kuchma's re-election in the October-November 1999 contest against Communist leader Petro Symonenko was marred by documented electoral fraud, using administrative resources and slanted media coverage to secure a second term.
consequential_events: Kuchma followed his re-election with an April 2000 constitutional referendum to grant himself power to dissolve parliament, passed amid further documented fraud, but the Verkhovna Rada refused to implement the changes.

precipitating_event: The February 2001 election gave the Party of Communists a two-thirds supermajority, and on April 4, 2001 parliament elected PCRM leader Vladimir Voronin president, concentrating both a constitutional supermajority and the presidency in one party for the first time since independence.
consequential_events: PCRM used its dominance of state media and administrative resources through the 2005 election cycle, entrenching one-party dominance even as Voronin pursued a pro-EU pivot after 2003.

precipitating_event: On June 5, 2000, the Malaita Eagle Force militia, backed by elements of the police, staged an armed coup, seizing PM Bartholomew Ulufa'alu at gunpoint and forcing his resignation.
consequential_events: Parliament installed Manasseh Sogavare as PM on June 30, 2000; the Townsville Peace Agreement (October 2000) granted amnesty and mandated disarmament, completed by mid-2001.

precipitating_event: Following Chavez's December 1998 election win, an April 1999 referendum approved a Constituent Assembly; the July 1999 assembly election gave Chavez's coalition a near-total supermajority, letting it unilaterally rewrite the constitution, ratified in a December 1999 referendum.
consequential_events: After two decades of enabling-act decree powers, court-packing, and an unconstitutional 2017 Constituent Assembly, the May 20, 2018 election, held on a truncated timeline with major opposition barred, gave Maduro 67.85% on 46% turnout and was rejected as fraudulent internationally.

precipitating_event: On 30 April 1999, Colonel Azali Assoumani led a bloodless military coup that ousted interim President Tadjidine Ben Said Massounde, suspending the constitution amid the Anjouan secession crisis.
consequential_events: Azali adopted a new "Fundamental Act" in May 1999 concentrating power in himself; he retained power past his pledged April 2000 deadline, continuing military-dominated rule through 2000.

precipitating_event: In 2002 President Bakili Muluzi and UDF allies pushed the "Open Terms Bill" to abolish presidential term limits so Muluzi could seek a third term, backed by state patronage and UDF dominance of campaign resources.
consequential_events: The bill was defeated in 2002-2003 amid protests; Muluzi then handpicked Bingu wa Mutharika as UDF successor, who won the disputed 2004 election, before breaking from UDF in February 2005 to found the DPP, personalizing power.

precipitating_event: President Ibrahim Bare Mainassara (himself a 1996 coup leader) was assassinated by his own Presidential Guard on 9 April 1999; Major Daouda Malam Wanke then seized power heading a military "National Reconciliation Council."
consequential_events: Wanke's junta adopted a new constitution in July 1999 and organized elections in October-November 1999, won by Mamadou Tandja; the junta transferred power to the elected civilian government by December 1999.

precipitating_event: On 12 October 1999, Army Chief Gen. Pervez Musharraf staged a bloodless coup after PM Nawaz Sharif tried to dismiss him while abroad; troops seized key institutions within 17 hours.
consequential_events: Musharraf declared a state of emergency on 14 October 1999 and issued a Provisional Constitutional Order suspending the constitution; the Supreme Court validated the takeover under the "doctrine of necessity" in 2000, granting a three-year window.

precipitating_event: On 24 December 1999, mutinying soldiers seized Abidjan's airport and ousted President Henri Konan Bedie; retired General Robert Guei was installed as head of a National Public Salvation Committee and publicly promised democracy would be respected.
consequential_events: The junta's constitution excluded opposition leader Alassane Ouattara from the presidential race; Guei tried to declare himself winner of the flawed October 2000 election, but a popular uprising forced him out and installed Laurent Gbagbo, inaugurated 26 October 2000.

precipitating_event: On 19 May 2000, businessman George Speight, backed by the army's Counter Revolutionary Warfare Unit, stormed Fiji's Parliament and took PM Mahendra Chaudhry's government hostage, declaring himself interim president.
consequential_events: Military commander Frank Bainimarama declared martial law after President Mara resigned; hostages were released via the Muanikau Accord, courts ruled the interim government illegal in November 2000, and elections were held in 2001, bringing Laisenia Qarase to power.

precipitating_event: Armed ethnic-Albanian NLA attacks on police/border posts began in late 2000, escalating on January 22, 2001 when NLA fighters attacked a police station near Tetovo, marking the start of the insurgency.
consequential_events: The General Ceasefire Agreement (July 2001) demilitarized conflict zones, and the Ohrid Framework Agreement (August 13, 2001) ended large-scale fighting via power-sharing and decentralization reforms.

precipitating_event: King Gyanendra dismissed elected PM Sher Bahadur Deuba, dissolved his government, and indefinitely postponed elections Deuba had called for, invoking royal reserve powers amid the Maoist civil war.
consequential_events: The King directly appointed and dismissed a succession of prime ministers without elections, entrenching personal royal control that set the stage for his outright 2005 coup.

precipitating_event: Jean-Bertrand Aristide was inaugurated to a second term in February 2001 following flawed May 2000 elections and an opposition boycott of the November 2000 presidential race; his government ruled with no meaningful opposition, backed by armed pro-government gangs.
consequential_events: An armed rebellion seized Gonaives and advanced on Port-au-Prince; on February 29, 2004 US officials escorted Aristide out of the country, ending his presidency with an interim government installed.

precipitating_event: During vote canvassing for the May 2004 election, President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo allegedly held wiretapped conversations discussing manipulation of returns to secure her win, revealed publicly in mid-2005 as the "Hello Garci" scandal.
consequential_events: A House impeachment complaint against Arroyo was blocked on September 6, 2005 by her coalition-dominated House despite polls showing most Filipinos believed she cheated, allowing her to consolidate power.

precipitating_event: The BNP government under PM Khaleda Zia launched "Operation Clean Heart," a nationwide crackdown that also targeted political opponents, detaining Awami League leaders, followed by an indemnity ordinance shielding security forces from prosecution.
consequential_events: A dispute over caretaker-government leadership triggered violent unrest and cancellation of the January 2007 election; the military installed Fakhruddin Ahmed's caretaker government under a state of emergency, remaining beyond its constitutional term.

precipitating_event: General Francois Bozize led fighters to seize Bangui while President Ange-Felix Patasse was abroad; rebels captured the airport and presidential palace with minimal resistance, forcing Patasse into exile.
consequential_events: Bozize proclaimed himself president, suspended the constitution, and formed a transitional "union government"; a new constitution was approved by referendum in December 2004, leading to elections in 2005 that Bozize won.

precipitating_event: President Charles Taylor resigned and went into exile on 11 August 2003 under military pressure from the LURD/MODEL rebel siege of Monrovia; the Accra Comprehensive Peace Agreement was signed about a week later, installing an unelected power-sharing transitional government.
consequential_events: The National Transitional Government of Liberia continued to rule without elections through 2004 while controlling little real territory, with UN peacekeeping/disarmament consolidating ahead of the October 2005 elections.

precipitating_event: On 19 September 2006, while PM Thaksin Shinawatra was in New York, General Sonthi Boonyaratglin led the Royal Thai Army in a coup, suspending the 1997 constitution and dissolving parliament and the Constitutional Court.
consequential_events: The junta installed an interim civilian PM, drafted a new constitution, dissolved Thaksin's party and banned its executives from politics, then held elections as promised on 23 December 2007.

precipitating_event: In June 2004, High Representative Paddy Ashdown used internationally granted "Bonn Powers" to dismiss 58 Bosnian public officials in a single day, an unelected international administrator overriding elected domestic institutions.
consequential_events: The US-brokered "April Package" constitutional reform failed in the House of Representatives by two votes in April 2006; the October 2006 election brought Milorad Dodik's SNSD to power in Republika Srpska on a platform resistant to further centralization.

precipitating_event: Mahinda Rajapaksa narrowly won the 17 November 2005 presidential election, aided by an LTTE-enforced boycott suppressing Tamil votes likely favoring his rival; Rajapaksa then allied with Sinhalese nationalist parties opposed to devolution and the peace process.
consequential_events: On 21 July 2006 the LTTE closed the Mavil Aru reservoir; the Sri Lankan military responded with an offensive, collapsing the 2002 ceasefire and returning the country to full-scale civil war, cementing war-footing centralization of power.

precipitating_event: Macedonia's 2005 local elections were marred by irregularities per international observers; the 5 July 2006 parliamentary election, won by Nikola Gruevski's VMRO-DPMNE coalition, began consolidating media and security-sector control.
consequential_events: By the early 2010s, after consecutive VMRO-DPMNE wins (2006, 2008, 2011), independent media access had shrunk sharply and Gruevski had installed loyalists atop the intelligence service, cementing one-party institutional capture.

precipitating_event: A 2007 military "e-memorandum" opposed AKP's presidential candidate, precipitating a snap election AKP won; on 21 October 2007 voters approved a referendum shifting presidential selection to direct popular vote, the first legal step in Erdogan's consolidation.
consequential_events: After the failed 15 July 2016 coup attempt, a state of emergency enabled mass dismissals of judges, officers, and civil servants; the 16 April 2017 referendum replaced the parliamentary system with an executive presidency.

precipitating_event: In January 2009 Bolivians approved a new constitution establishing a centralized "plurinational state"; Morales later moved to eliminate term limits, culminating in a November 2017 Constitutional Tribunal ruling permitting unlimited reelection despite a 2016 referendum rejecting this.
consequential_events: Morales resigned November 2019 amid a disputed election that an OAS audit found showed "sufficient evidence of election fraud"; Senator Jeanine Anez assumed the presidency without quorum, and elections were finally held October 2020.

precipitating_event: On 5 December 2006, military forces led by Commodore Frank Bainimarama seized government buildings and placed ministers of PM Laisenia Qarase's government under house arrest, ousting the elected government.
consequential_events: President Iloilo, reinstated January 2007, formally appointed Bainimarama as interim prime minister, installing a military-backed government that indefinitely postponed elections until 2014.

precipitating_event: Acting on a sealed Supreme Court arrest warrant over President Manuel Zelaya's push for a referendum on a constitutional assembly, soldiers stormed the presidential residence on 28 June 2009, detained Zelaya, and flew him into exile.
consequential_events: Congress installed its president Roberto Micheletti as interim leader and allowed the previously scheduled November 2009 elections to proceed; Porfirio Lobo won and was inaugurated January 2010.

precipitating_event: In the April 2010 election, Viktor Orban's Fidesz won a two-thirds supermajority, used to draft a new Fundamental Law behind closed doors, debated for only nine days and passed on a party-line vote; the constitution took effect 1 January 2012.
consequential_events: Over the following decade Fidesz redrew electoral districts, installed loyalists on media and courts, and transferred control of state universities to Orban-aligned foundations; Orban's 16-year rule ended when Fidesz lost the April 2026 election.

precipitating_event: After Hamas's forcible takeover of Gaza in June 2007, President Mahmoud Abbas declared a state of emergency on 14 June 2007, dissolved the Hamas-led unity government, and installed Salam Fayyad as PM by decree, bypassing the Hamas-majority legislature.
consequential_events: The Fayyad emergency government continued ruling the West Bank by decree with the legislature no longer functioning; Abbas's presidential term was extended without new elections.

precipitating_event: Constituent Assembly elections held 30 September 2007 gave Rafael Correa's PAIS Alliance a large majority; when the Assembly convened in November 2007 it assumed plenary powers superseding the sitting opposition-controlled Congress.
consequential_events: Ecuadorians approved a new constitution in a September 2008 referendum expanding presidential decree powers, after Congress had already voted to remove all nine Constitutional Court judges; Correa was re-elected by landslide in 2013.

precipitating_event: While PM Michael Somare was hospitalized abroad, Parliament declared his office vacant in August 2011 and elected Peter O'Neill prime minister, triggering a dispute over who legitimately held executive power.
consequential_events: After the Supreme Court twice ruled Somare remained the lawful PM, the O'Neill government defied the rulings, had the Chief Justice arrested on sedition charges, and survived a January 2012 mutiny attempt; the crisis was settled by the 2012 general election.

precipitating_event: In the run-up to the 19 December 2012 election, National Intelligence Service agents covertly posted online comments and coordinated conservative civic groups to boost ruling-party candidate Park Geun-hye and disparage rival Moon Jae-in.
consequential_events: A prosecutorial raid on NIS headquarters led to the indictment of NIS director Won Sei-hoon and Seoul's police chief for election interference, but Won's conviction came long after Park had already taken office.

precipitating_event: On 21 March 2012, mutinying soldiers led by Captain Amadou Sanogo, angered by the government's handling of the Tuareg rebellion, stormed the presidential palace and seized power.
consequential_events: President Amadou Toumani Toure resigned 8 April 2012; the junta transferred power to interim civilian leadership, and after a French-backed military intervention, Ibrahim Boubacar Keita won the July-August 2013 election.

precipitating_event: On 17 September 2019, Indonesia's parliament, with President Jokowi's backing, passed a hastily deliberated revision to the KPK law that stripped the Corruption Eradication Commission of independent investigative authority.
consequential_events: In October 2023, the Constitutional Court chaired by Jokowi's brother-in-law carved out an age-limit exception letting Jokowi's son Gibran run for vice president; Prabowo-Gibran won the February 2024 election and were inaugurated October 2024.

precipitating_event: Narendra Modi's BJP won an outright parliamentary majority in May 2014, beginning a trajectory that, especially after 2019 re-election, saw sedition/anti-terror laws and agencies increasingly deployed against opposition figures amid a reshaped pro-government media landscape.
consequential_events: The August 2019 revocation of Jammu and Kashmir's special autonomy, and the 2018 Electoral Bonds funding scheme (struck down by the Supreme Court in February 2024), were landmark aggrandizing moves; V-Dem downgraded India to "electoral autocracy" in 2021.

precipitating_event: After weeks of opposition protests led by Antananarivo mayor Andry Rajoelina against President Marc Ravalomanana, the military stormed the presidential palace on 16 March 2009 and forced Ravalomanana to hand power to a military directorate, which transferred it to Rajoelina.
consequential_events: Rajoelina was sworn in as president of a High Transitional Authority on 21 March 2009; the African Union suspended Madagascar and called the takeover an "attempted coup," and promised elections were repeatedly delayed until 2013.

precipitating_event: On 20 June 2009, President Mamadou Tandja assumed "special powers" and pushed through an illegal constitutional referendum removing presidential term limits, after the Constitutional Court ruled the referendum illegal and he dissolved the National Assembly.
consequential_events: On 18 February 2010, a military junta led by Col. Salou Djibo ousted Tandja; the junta publicly promised elections and restored civilian democratic rule, culminating in Mahamadou Issoufou's March 2011 inauguration.

precipitating_event: In the July 2010 election, Pierre Nkurunziza ran unopposed after opposition parties boycotted the vote citing fraud in preceding communal elections, cementing CNDD-FDD's uncontested dominance.
consequential_events: After Nkurunziza announced a third-term bid in April 2015, validated by the Constitutional Court despite Arusha Accords term limits, a failed May 2015 military coup was followed by a violent crackdown; Nkurunziza won a boycotted July 2015 election.

precipitating_event: On 7 February 2012, President Mohamed Nasheed resigned amid a 22-day opposition protest and a mutiny in which police joined demonstrators following his controversial arrest of the Chief Justice; VP Mohamed Waheed assumed power in what Nasheed called a coup, though an inquiry found no supporting evidence.
consequential_events: Abdulla Yameen won the November 2013 runoff and from 2014-2017 jailed opposition leaders and Supreme Court justices, imposed states of emergency, and blocked opposition parties from contesting elections.

precipitating_event: In the May 2012 elections, Tomislav Nikolic won the presidency and the SNS-led coalition topped parliamentary elections, bringing Aleksandar Vucic into the center of power; SNS subsequently built dominance over media and state institutions.
consequential_events: Freedom House downgraded Serbia from "Free" to "Partly Free" in 2019 and reclassified it a "hybrid regime" in 2020; disputed 2020, 2023, and 2024 elections and mass protests in 2024-2025 have continued amid documented irregularities favoring the ruling party.

precipitating_event: On 1 October 2010, Ukraine's Constitutional Court, packed with Yanukovych loyalists, annulled the 2004 constitutional reforms and restored the strong presidential system of the 2006 constitution, removing "the last legal obstacle" to concentration of power by President Yanukovych.
consequential_events: After Yanukovych's November 2013 refusal to sign the EU Association Agreement sparked the Euromaidan protests and nearly 100 protesters were killed in February 2014, he fled Kyiv on 21 February 2014 and parliament voted to remove him the next day.
